text: Jacques Fabien Gautier d'Agoty and his sons popularised colour engraving in France. He was a pupil of Jacob Christoph Le Blon, who invented the first colour printing process, with blue, yellow and red. D'Agoty claimed he had proposed an improved method using black and was rebuffed. For many years the family published a journal with colour illustrations. He is best remembered for the anatomical charts he made with the physician Guichard Joseph Duverney, including a Myologie complète in colour and life size in 1746. The tendons and veins stood out in what was called horrible precision.

John William Wright grew up in a family of miniaturists. His father, John Wright, was a miniature painter of repute, and his mother Priscilla was also a good miniaturist, but she died when he was an infant. Ill health followed him all his life, and he had to leave school at Loughborough House in Brixton. He was apprenticed to Thomas Phillips and from 1825 often exhibited at the Royal Academy, mainly portraits. In 1842 he became a full member of the Old Watercolour Society.

When Justus van Huysum turned 16, his father sent him to learn painting from Nicolaes Berchem. According to Houbraken, he was good at all sorts of painting but excelled at flowers, and he founded a family business painting flowers in vases. His father, Jan van Huysum the Elder, was a decorative painter, and his brother Caspar became an engraver. Justus decorated rooms in many Dutch houses with the help of his three sons. He painted portraits, landscapes, seascapes and flowers.

Pavel Tretyakov bought Pavel Svedomsky's painting Medusa for his gallery. Svedomsky was born in St Petersburg into the hereditary Russian nobility and spent his childhood with his brother Alexander on the family estate in Perm. In 1870 he entered the Düsseldorf Academy but stayed only a few months, then studied in Munich under Eduard von Gebhardt and Mihály Munkácsy. The brothers travelled across Europe together until they settled in Rome in 1875. Pavel also painted six scenes from the life of Jesus in St Volodymyr's Cathedral in Kiev. He and Alexander are buried together in Rome's Protestant Cemetery.

Peter Paul Benazech trained under François Vivares and worked as a draughtsman and engraver in both London and Paris. His best engravings are landscapes and marine subjects after Dietrich and Vernet. He also engraved a series of anatomical plates and a set of seven scenes from the Seven Years' War. With Pierre-Charles Canot he made four plates of engagements between the English and French fleets after Francis Swaine. His latest dated plate is from 1783. His son Charles became a notable portrait and history painter.

Will Henry Stevens learned to grind and mix his own paints from his father, an apothecary in Vevay, Indiana. Those skills later let him develop new formulas for pastel chalks. He studied at the Cincinnati Art Academy for three years, then began work as a painter and designer at Rookwood Pottery in 1904. He is known for tonal pastels of the rural Southern landscape, abstractions of nature, and non-objective works. His paintings are in over forty US museums, including the Ogden Museum of Southern Art and the Museum of Fine Arts Boston.

Petrus Marius Molijn was born in Rotterdam but spent much of his career in Antwerp, where he studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts under Ferdinand De Braekeleer and Henri Leys. He painted landscapes, interiors and still lifes. He also worked as an etcher and lithographer. In 1845 the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Amsterdam named him a member. He died aged only twenty-nine. A small monument to him stands in Antwerp.

Simó Gómez went to Paris at seventeen to work in a lithographer's workshop but decided to become a painter instead. In Barcelona he had studied at the Escola de la Llotja under Ramón Martí Alsina. To prepare for the entrance exam of the École des Beaux-arts, he worked in the studios of Alexandre Cabanel and Tony Robert-Fleury and copied the classics in the museums. There he gave up the Academicism of his early years for Realism, with Manet and Delacroix as strong influences. When his family's money ran out, his teachers petitioned Queen Isabella II on his behalf.

Kobayashi Kiyochika documented Japan's rapid modernization in the Meiji period in woodblock prints and newspaper illustrations. He used a sense of light and shade inspired by Western art. His work first found an audience in the 1870s with prints of red-brick buildings and trains. His prints of the First Sino-Japanese War were popular too. Many collectors consider his work the last significant example of ukiyo-e. He was born Kobayashi Katsunosuke in Edo's Honjo neighborhood, and his father was a minor official in charge of unloading rice collected as taxes.

Claude-Joseph Vernet helped his father Antoine, a skilled decorative painter, with the most important parts of his work at only fourteen. Painting the panels of sedan chairs could not satisfy his ambition, so he left for Rome. The whales he saw at Marseille and the voyage to Civitavecchia made a deep impression on him. In Rome he entered the studios of the whale painter Bernardino Fergioni and the marine landscapist Adrien Manglard, who introduced him to seascape painting. He also studied landscape designers and maritime painters such as Claude Lorrain. His son Carle and daughter Marguerite Émilie were painters too.

Otto van Veen taught the young Rubens in the 1590s. He was a painter, draughtsman and humanist who ran a large workshop in Antwerp and designed several emblem books. His role as a classically educated humanist artist influenced Rubens, who took on that role himself. He was born in Leiden, the son of the burgomaster Cornelis Jansz. van Veen. He became court painter to successive governors of the Habsburg Netherlands, including the Archdukes Albert and Isabella.

Jacob Folkema was born and died in Dokkum in Friesland. His father, a goldsmith, taught him first, and he later studied under B. Picart in Amsterdam. During that time he worked on Royaumont's Bible in 1712 and Ruysch's Anatomy in 1737. He was also an excellent engraver in mezzotint. His sister Anna painted miniatures, assisted him and engraved a few plates.

Julius Mařák wavered between art and music. Several relatives were singers and musicians, and he was born in Litomyšl to an auditor and land registrar. He studied in Prague under Max Haushofer, then in Munich under Leopold Rottmann and Eduard Schleich. After wandering through Bohemia he settled in Vienna, where he learned etching, gave drawing lessons and illustrated local magazines. Barbizon influences appeared in his work although he had never been to France. In 1887 Josef Hlávka offered him a professorship for landscape painting in Prague.

Willem Pieter Hoevenaar learned to paint from his father, Adriaenus Hoevenaar, and later from Pieter Christoffel Wonder. His brothers Cornelis Willem and Nicolaas Ludolph were painters too. His works were shown at exhibitions in The Hague and Amsterdam from 1828 to 1863, and his sepia drawings were popular in his time. His pupils included David van der Kellen Jr. and his son Jozef, who drew his portrait. He is known for genre works with figures, often in vintage Dutch costumes.

The son of a crofter, William McTaggart came from the small village of Aros near Campbeltown in Kintyre. He moved to Edinburgh at 16 and studied at the Trustees' Academy under Robert Scott Lauder, winning several prizes. He became a full member of the Royal Scottish Academy in 1870. His early works were mainly figure paintings, often of children, but he later turned to landscape and seascape, inspired by his childhood love of the sea. He adopted the Impressionist practice of painting out of doors and tried to capture the changing effects of light on water.

Hofstede de Groot claimed Nicolaes Berchem painted around 850 pictures, though many are misattributed. His 80 etchings and 500 drawings were also in great demand. He belonged to the second generation of Dutch Italianate landscape painters, artists who travelled to Italy, or hoped to, and brought home sketchbooks of classical ruins and pastoral scenes. His idealised rural landscapes show hills and trees in a golden dawn. He also painted the figures and animals in works by other artists, such as Allaert van Everdingen, Jan Hackaert, Gerrit Dou and Meindert Hobbema.

Henri Harpignies' parents wanted him in business, but his determination to become an artist was so strong that at 27 he entered Jean Achard's atelier in Paris. Achard gave him sound constructive draughtsmanship. After two years he went to Italy, returning in 1850. He then painted children in landscape settings and fell in with Corot and the other Barbizon masters. His main exhibited works were oils, yet by French standards he took watercolour unusually seriously, and he was also a printmaker.

According to Houbraken, Cornelis Brouwer was a pupil of Rembrandt and a friend of Eglon van der Neer. In 1676 he helped the seventeen-year-old Adriaen van der Werff by showing his self-portrait to all his art friends in Rotterdam, who were amazed at such ability in a young man. The RKD knows him for genre works and historical allegories of the Rembrandt school. He is sometimes confused with Justus Brouwer. Brouwer came from Rotterdam and died there in 1681.

Sawrey Gilpin was sent to London at fourteen to study under the marine painter Samuel Scott, but he preferred sketching the market carts and horses that passed by. It soon became clear that animals, especially horses, were his speciality. He left Scott in 1758 and devoted himself to animal painting. Born in Carlisle, he was the seventh child of Captain John Bernard Gilpin, who ran a drawing school there. His elder brother William wrote influential works on picturesque scenery. Sawrey was made a Royal Academician.

Richard Parkes Bonington's family moved to France when he was 14, so he can also be considered a French artist, an intermediary bringing aspects of English style to France. His landscapes were mostly coastal scenes with a low horizon and a large sky, showing a brilliant handling of light and atmosphere. In his last years he also painted small historical cabinet paintings in a freely handled version of the troubadour style. He worked in oils and watercolour. After his early death in 1828, he became one of the most influential British artists of his time.

Paulus Pontius was apprenticed in Antwerp to the still life painter Osias Beert on 3 December 1616. He later learned engraving from Lucas Vorsterman, Rubens' primary engraver. Together with Vorsterman, Schelte a Bolswert and Boetius à Bolswert, he became one of the leading engravers of the first generation who made reproductions after Rubens. When Vorsterman left for England in 1624 after a conflict with Rubens, Pontius took over. After Rubens' death he worked with other leading Antwerp painters such as Anthony van Dyck and Jacob Jordaens.

Maxime Lalanne studied law and worked as a notary's clerk, even though his comrades and teachers noticed his artistic talent. His father was a civil servant in Bordeaux who rose to clerk of the first chamber of the Court of Appeals. Lalanne drew in his spare time. In 1850 he exhibited six drawings in pencil and pastel at the Philomathique Society's exhibition in the Palais de Justice. Léo Drouyn noticed his work. Lalanne became known for his etchings and charcoal drawings.

Léon Spilliaert moved among the Belgian symbolist writers, of whom Maurice Maeterlinck and Émile Verhaeren were the best known. Edvard Munch and Edgar Allan Poe were among those who inspired his work. He was born in Ostend, the oldest of seven children of a perfumer. His subjects ranged from self-portraits and marines to forest views, airships and dolls. He also illustrated many literary works. His style is marked by tenebrism and simplicity of form, and by a bitter, mysterious expression in his characters and landscapes.

Jakob Becker began working as a lithographer at 17, after his first studies with Franz Nikolaus Jung in Worms. His first important work was a panorama of the Rhine from Mainz to Cologne. He studied at the Düsseldorf Academy between 1833 and 1841 under Johann Wilhelm Schirmer and Wilhelm von Schadow. In 1842 he became professor of genre and landscape painting at the Städelschule in Frankfurt. There he broke with the lofty attitude of Biblical history painting, sought his subjects in the countryside and took a special interest in the social problems of the peasantry.

Sebastian Sierakowski helped establish the Astronomical Observatory of Lwów University in 1771 and became its first director. He had studied in Lwów, Vienna and Rome. He was ordained in Rome. Then he taught mathematics and astronomy. When the Jesuit Order was suppressed in 1773, he went to Kraków and became a canon at Wawel Cathedral. In 1787 he drew up a restoration plan for Wawel Castle for the arrival of Stanisław August Poniatowski.

Eero Järnefelt's sister Aino became the wife of Jean Sibelius. He came from a Swedish-speaking Finnophile family of artists and writers, and his brothers included a literary critic, a judge and writer, and the composer Armas. As a Finnish painter he is best known for portraits and landscapes of the area around Koli National Park in North Karelia. He won medals at the Paris Exposition Universelle in 1889 and 1900. Järnefelt taught art at the University of Helsinki and chaired the Finnish Academy of Fine Arts.

Edward Penfield is considered the father of the American poster. He studied at New York's Art Students League and worked under George de Forest Brush. He first worked for Harper's Weekly and later became its art director. His style used simplified figures with bold outlines in settings free of extraneous detail. He believed that a design that needs study is not a poster, no matter how well executed. He also wrote and published Holland Sketches.

J. Alden Weir grew up at West Point, where his father, the painter Robert Walter Weir, taught drawing at the Military Academy for forty years, with pupils such as Whistler and Robert E. Lee. Weir was the second to last of sixteen children, and his older brother John Ferguson Weir became a well-known landscape artist. As an American impressionist, he belonged to the Cos Cob Art Colony in Greenwich, Connecticut. In 1898 he helped found The Ten, a group of artists dissatisfied with professional art organizations who exhibited together.

A bookstore may have shaped Samuel Colman's career. His father opened one in New York City, where the family moved when Colman was a child, and its literate clientele may have influenced him. Colman is believed to have studied briefly under Asher Durand and exhibited his first work at the National Academy of Design in 1850. He became a full member of the Academy in 1862. His landscapes of the 1850s were influenced by the Hudson River School, as in Meadows and Wildflowers at Conway from 1856. He was also an interior designer and a writer.

John Lavery used insurance money from a fire to study in London. His first studio in Glasgow, set up in 1878, was razed the following year, and the £300 pay-out paid for a year at Heatherley's School. He was born in Belfast and orphaned young after his father drowned in the sinking of the packet ship Pomona. He attended the Haldane Academy in Glasgow and continued his studies at the Académie Julian in Paris. He is best known for portraits and wartime depictions.

Remigius Adrianus Haanen, also called Remy van Haanen, came from Oosterhout in the Netherlands. His father, the papercutter Casparis Haanen, taught him his trade, and he then studied at the Academy of Utrecht. His brother George Gillis and his sisters Elisabeth Alida and Adriana Johanna were painters too. In 1837 he moved to Austria and worked in Vienna. He died in Bad Aussee in 1894.

Ernst Willem Jan Bagelaar, born in Eindhoven, first entered the army, but he acquired a liking for the fine arts and taught himself etching. He learned more by travelling through Germany and staying in Paris. Giving up soldiering, he retired to his property at Zon, near Eindhoven, where he died in 1837. His etchings are numerous and executed in imitation of drawings. Many are landscapes from his own designs. The style of Jan Luyken had a special charm for him, and he owned a considerable collection of Luyken's drawings.

Léon Davent signed most of his prints only with the letters L.D., and older literature knows him as the Master L.D. Lists of his work attribute between 98 and 226 prints to him. He was a French printmaker, closely tied to the First School of Fontainebleau, who worked in both engraving and etching. Many of his prints follow designs by Francesco Primaticcio, rendered boldly and freely. His dated prints run from 1540 to 1556. Very little else is known about his life.

Juliusz Kossak founded an artistic family that spanned four generations. He grew up in Lwów and took a law degree to please his mother, while studying painting with Jan Maszkowski and Piotr Michałowski. From 1844 he worked on commissions for the local aristocracy. After marrying Zofia Gałczyńska in 1855, he left with her for Paris, where they spent five years and where their twin sons Wojciech and Tadeusz were born. The family moved to Warsaw in 1860. He specialised in battle scenes, military portraits and horses.

George Chinnery spent most of his life in Asia, especially India and southern China. He was born in London and studied at the Royal Academy Schools. In 1796 he moved to Ireland, where he enjoyed some success as an artist and married Marianne Vigne. He returned to London in 1801 without his wife and two infant children. The next year he sailed to Madras. He established himself as a painter there and then in Calcutta, where he became the leading artist of the British community in India.

Edward Francis Burney's cousin was the novelist Fanny Burney, and his uncle the musicologist Charles Burney. He studied at the Royal Academy Schools from 1776, where Sir Joshua Reynolds encouraged him. His portrait of his cousin Frances was engraved as a frontispiece to her works. He also exhibited three drawings illustrating her novel Evelina, which were engraved for an edition of 1791. Much of his work was book illustration, including a series for an edition of Milton's Paradise Lost. He later painted four satirical watercolours.

Peter Ilsted's sister Ida married the painter Vilhelm Hammershøi in 1891. He is best known for domestic interiors. Ilsted came to the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts in 1878 and finished his course in five years. He made his debut at the Charlottenborg Spring Exhibition in 1883. Later he joined a study trip across Italy to Egypt, Palestine, Greece and Turkey, and he visited several other countries.

Jan Lievens and Rembrandt shared a studio for about five years until 1631. Both had trained with Pieter Lastman in Amsterdam. According to Houbraken, Lievens was the son of an embroiderer and was sent to Lastman at about ten for two full years. He began working as an independent artist in Leiden at about twelve and became something of a celebrity for his talent at such a young age. Unlike Rembrandt, whose career stayed in Amsterdam, Lievens worked in London, Antwerp, The Hague and Berlin.

Early in his career Thomas Bewick engraved cutlery and made wood blocks for advertisements. He was apprenticed to the engraver Ralph Beilby in Newcastle upon Tyne, became a partner in the business, and eventually took it over. His A History of Quadrupeds won him an adult audience for its fine illustrations. He is best known for A History of British Birds, admired today mainly for its wood engravings, especially the small, sharply observed and often humorous vignettes called tail-pieces. The book was the forerunner of all modern field guides.

Johann Heinrich Roos was born in Otterberg in the Palatinate, and the Thirty Years' War drove his family to Amsterdam. He trained with Guilliam du Gardijn, Cornelis de Bie and Barent Graat, but Nicolaes Berchem and Karel Dujardin influenced him more. When the family returned to Germany in 1653, he and his brother Theodor worked together on a commission for a cloister in Mainz. In 1664 he was invited to paint at the court of the Elector Palatine. Unsatisfactory working conditions made him move to Frankfurt in 1667, where he was very successful.

Tina Blau's father, a doctor, strongly supported her wish to become a painter. She took lessons in Munich from August Schaeffer and Wilhelm Lindenschmit, and she also studied with Emil Jakob Schindler. They shared a studio for a year, but the engagement allegedly ended after a quarrel. In 1883 she converted from Judaism to the Evangelical Lutheran Church and married Heinrich Lang, a painter of horses and battle scenes. From 1889 she taught landscape and still life painting at the Women's Academy in Munich. She exhibited at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893.

Marco Dente was killed in the tumult of the Sack of Rome in 1527. Born in Ravenna, he belonged to the circle of printmakers around Marcantonio Raimondi in Rome, and most of his output was reproductive prints or close copies of other prints. Some of them are of special interest because they show sculptural restorations. He used a monogram, D-B, but only sparingly. Debate over attributions within Raimondi's school, and the destruction of every plate in Dente's studio, blurred his identity.

Richard Westall was Queen Victoria's drawing master. He is best known today for his portraits of Byron. His attempts to introduce heroic and patriotic subjects to the English watercolour tradition failed even in his own lifetime, after an early success, but his works were widely reproduced as prints. He was born in Reepham near Norwich and moved to London after his mother's death and his father's bankruptcy in 1772. He was apprenticed to a heraldic silver engraver in 1779. His younger half-brother William was a much-travelled landscape painter.

When Willem Bastiaan Tholen was five, his family moved to Kampen. There he became friends with the young Jan Voerman, and they entered the Amsterdam academy together in 1876. Tholen earned his certificate of proficiency within a year and then attended drawing classes at the Polytechnic School in Delft for two years. After he got a secondary school teaching certificate in 1878, he worked as a drawing instructor at the evening secondary school in Gouda. He spent three months in Brussels in the studio of Paul Gabriël, from whom he received his first real instruction in painting.

Théodore Ralli came from the wealthy Greek Ralli family, one of the most successful Greek merchant families of the 19th century, with operations spanning the entire world. Born in Constantinople, he spent most of his working life in France and Greece, with years in Egypt as well. He painted in an Academic, Orientalist and Impressionist manner and is known for orientalist scenes and pictures of Greek everyday life. He studied with Jean-Léon Gérôme. A dissertation by Maria Katsanaki in 2007 catalogues over 400 paintings attributed to him, and most of his works are in private collections.

Jacob Maris belonged to the Hague School of painters together with his brothers Willem and Matthijs. He was considered the most important and influential Dutch landscape painter of the last quarter of the nineteenth century. His first teacher was J.A.B. Stroebel, and he then enrolled at the Hague Academy of Art. An art dealer recognised his talent and got him into the studio of Hubertus van Hove. He is best known for a series of portraits of the House of Orange, made with Matthijs, and for landscapes such as Ship on the Scheveningen beach.

Johan Gabriëlse became best known for his school plates of the Dutch East Indies, published by Wolters. He studied at the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam under August Allebé and Nicolaas van der Waay. He also illustrated school books, designed book covers and painted many oil paintings. He taught his daughter Corrie. Japanese forces interned him because of his artworks, and he died of exhaustion in the St. Louis camp at Ambarawa on Java in 1945.

Johann Cyriak Hackhofer is regarded as the most important Baroque monumental painter of Styria. He was born in Wilten near Innsbruck, the son of the organist of the Wilten abbey. He worked in Vienna from 1704 and from 1708 until his death served as court painter to Vorau Abbey and its parishes. Egid Schor and the Waldmanns in Tyrol, and Johann Michael Rottmayr in Vienna, probably influenced him. He painted frescoes in the chapter house and sacristy at Vorau, in the market church and in six chapels, and he made the high altar painting for the parish church in Hartberg.

Yao Shou painted for pleasure rather than as a trade. He was born in 1423 in Jiashan in Zhejiang, the son of Yao Fu, a collector of calligraphy and painting. He passed the triennial examinations in the capital and received the degree of jinshi. Like his fellow scholar-painter Liu Jue, he was a calligrapher and poet, and he took his inspiration from the Yuan masters. He admired Zhao Mengfu for his fidelity to the spirit of Antiquity. Yao Shou died in 1495.

Théodore Delachaux wrote a book on plankton at eleven, illustrated with drawings from his own microscope studies. His father was a doctor who introduced him early to natural science, and his maternal grandfather was the entomologist and botanist Charles Henri Godet. He went to school in Neuchâtel and lived with his uncle Paul Godet, director of the Natural History Museum, who continued his scientific education. Afterwards he studied at the École des beaux-arts in Paris under Luc-Olivier Merson. He returned to Neuchâtel in 1912. He worked as a teacher, painter, curator and ethnologist.

Francis Wheatley was the son of a master tailor from Covent Garden. His father placed him with a drawing teacher, and he then studied at William Shipley's drawing school before entering the Royal Academy in 1769. In his youth he often copied John Hamilton Mortimer, whom he helped paint decorations at Brocket Hall. He also worked on the decorations at Vauxhall. He exhibited a small portrait at the Incorporated Society of Artists as early as 1765, and he became the society's director in 1772.

Johann Christoph Sysang first learned his father's trade of ornamental turning, then took up engraving as an apprentice of the Leipzig engraver Martin Bernigeroth. In 1724 he set out as a journeyman, working for the university in Halle and passing through Dresden to Prague. He stayed five years in Prague and mostly engraved holy pictures. Back in Leipzig he became a sought-after engraver of portraits of princes, statesmen, doctors, jurists and theologians. From 1741 he contributed vignettes to Johann Heinrich Zedler's Universal-Lexikon.

Salomon Kleiner's mother died soon after his birth. At 15 or 16 he became an apprentice to the Augsburg engraver Johann August Corvinus. From 1720 he lived in Vienna, where he began drawing monasteries, churches and secular buildings for the Augsburg publishers Johann Andreas Pfeffel and Jeremias Wolff. Their engravings came out between 1724 and 1737 in a large series of Vienna views. He left Vienna for long only for one commission, from Lothar Franz von Schönborn, to draw the Schönborn palaces at Pommersfelden and Mainz.

Chōbunsai Eishi began by studying painting in the aristocratic Kanō school alongside the future shogun Tokugawa Ieharu. He then became official painter to that shogun and to his successor Ienari, which gave him a comfortable income for nearly three years. As shogun's painter he could not practise the more popular ukiyo-e, so around the age of thirty he gave up his post to devote himself to printmaking. Later he returned to court and to academic Kanō painting. Like Utamaro, he painted bijin-ga, pictures of beautiful people.

Vinzenz Katzler has had a street named after him in Vienna's Simmering district since 1956. He studied at the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts for four years. After 1848 he made portraits and illustrations for Figaro, Kikeriki, Hans Jörgel and the Leipziger Illustrirte. He is especially known for numerous woodcuts and lithographs, among them scenes of current events and motifs from the folk life of the Austrian monarchy.

Louis Ducros was the son of a drawing master at the Yverdon College. He was born in Moudon and came to Geneva in 1769 to study under Nicolas-Henri-Joseph de Fassin. Later he left for Italy and settled in Rome. In 1778 two Dutch noblemen hired him to accompany them on a four-month journey through the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and Malta, where he made almost three hundred watercolours, now in the Rijksmuseum. He worked in Rome as a landscape painter. In 1780 he published twenty-four views of Rome and its surroundings with the engraver Giovanni Volpato.

Nicolas-André Monsiau turned to book illustration when the French Revolution disrupted patronage. He trained at the school of the Académie royale under Jean-François Pierre Peyron, and an early patron, the marquis de Corberon, paid for a stay in Rome, where he studied at the French Academy from 1776. Back in Paris he was received at the Académie with Alexander taming Bucephalus and made a member in 1787 on the strength of The Death of Agis. His best-known painting is Zeuxis choosing among the most beautiful girls of Crotona, shown at the Salon of 1791.

Reza Abbasi spent most of his career working for Shah Abbas I and is considered the last great master of the Persian miniature. He is best known for single miniatures for albums, especially single figures of beautiful youths. His father, Ali Asghar, was also a miniature artist. Unlike most earlier Persian artists, Reza typically signed his work and often added dates. Scholars now reject many of those signatures. His first dated drawing is from 1601 and is in the Topkapi Palace.

Robert Smirke specialised in small paintings of subjects taken from literature, especially the English poets such as James Thomson. He was born at Wigton near Carlisle, the son of a travelling artist. At twelve he was apprenticed to a heraldic painter in London, and at twenty he began to study at the Royal Academy Schools. The Academy elected him an associate in 1791 and a full academician in 1793. In 1804 he was nominated keeper of the Academy, but George III refused the appointment because of his revolutionary political opinions.

Mariano Fortuny was orphaned young and raised by his grandfather, a cabinet-maker who taught him to make wax figurines. At nine, a public competition in his town brought him the encouragement of a local painter, Domènec Soberano. At fourteen he moved to Barcelona with his grandfather, and the sculptor Domènec Talarn secured him a pension to attend the Escola de la Llotja. In 1859 the province of Barcelona sent him to Morocco to depict the Spanish-Moroccan War. His sketches there later served for his monumental Battle of Tetuan.

Thorsten Waenerberg's sister Elin Kallio became known as the mother of Finnish women's gymnastics. He was the son of a theologian and studied first at the drawing school of the Finnish Art Society. In Karlsruhe he studied under Hans Fredrik Gude, and in 1866 he moved to Düsseldorf, where he stayed until 1873. There he was a pupil of Karl Müller. He also attended Oswald Achenbach's landscape class. He painted landscapes and marine scenes of the Düsseldorf school and worked as an art teacher and curator.

Willem Wenckebach is best known for his watercolours for the Verkade albums of Jac Thijsse, which he made with Jan Voerman junior and Jan van Oort. In Amsterdam he is also remembered for the many pen drawings of old Amsterdam that he made between 1898 and 1907 for the newspaper Het Nieuws van den Dag, later published again in book form. Wenckebach was born in The Hague. He did both applied and free work and became one of the best-known and most productive illustrators of his time.
